questions.q: According to Kirchhoff and Bunsen, which kind of object produces a continuous blackbody spectrum rather than an emission or absorption spectrum?
options: An incandescent low-density gas glowing on its own
A hot solid, liquid or dense gas under pressure, such as the inner layers of a star
A cool gas in front of a continuous source
The cool atmosphere of a star
questions.explanation: Kirchhoff and Bunsen found a continuous spectrum is produced by glowing solids, liquids or dense gases under pressure (which behave like black body radiators), such as the inner layers of stars. Incandescent low-density gases give emission lines, and cool gases in front of a continuous source give absorption lines.

questions.q: Why does a star such as the Sun produce an absorption spectrum rather than an emission spectrum?
options: The Sun is a hot gas, and all hot gases produce emission lines
The hot dense plasma at the centre produces a continuous spectrum, and the cooler atmosphere absorbs specific frequencies on the way out, cutting dark lines into the continuum
The cool atmosphere emits bright lines that overwhelm the continuous spectrum
The Sun is too distant for the continuous spectrum to reach us
questions.explanation: The hot dense plasma at the centre of a star produces a continuous blackbody spectrum; as that light moves outward, the gases in the star's cooler atmosphere absorb their characteristic frequencies, producing an absorption spectrum. The trap is to call the Sun 'a hot gas' and predict emission lines — a hot DENSE body gives a continuous spectrum, so density, not just temperature, is the deciding factor.

questions.q: State the three rules Kirchhoff and Bunsen established in 1859 for which type of spectrum a source produces.
keyPoints: A continuous colour spectrum is produced by glowing solids or dense gaseous bodies (such as the Sun), behaving like black body radiation.
If a gas lies between the continuous light source and the spectroscope, light is absorbed at wavelengths characteristic of the chemical components of the gas (absorption spectrum).
A glowing gas produces bright lines on a dark background at wavelengths characteristic of the chemical components of the gas (emission spectrum).
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three Kirchhoff–Bunsen rules and tied the absorption and emission lines to the characteristic wavelengths of the gas's chemical components, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: The spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M are arranged in order of what, and where does the Sun sit?
options: In order of abundance, with the Sun as a blue class O star
Alphabetically, with the Sun as a red class M star
In order of surface temperature from hottest (O, blue) to coolest (M, red), with the Sun a yellow class G star
In order of distance from Earth, with the Sun as a white class A star
questions.explanation: The classes are arranged by surface temperature, from O the hottest (blue, peaking in the ultraviolet) to M the coolest (red, peaking in the infra-red). The Sun is a type G star and these are yellow. The odd-looking order arose because the letters were assigned before the temperature ordering was understood — recall the mnemonic 'Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me'.

questions.q: What does the colour of a star tell an astronomer, and how does wavelength relate to temperature?
options: Colour gives the star's distance; hotter stars look redder
Colour indicates the surface temperature; hotter stars radiate more energy at short (blue) wavelengths, cooler stars at longer (red) wavelengths
Colour gives the star's chemical composition directly, independent of temperature
Colour gives the star's velocity; bluer stars are always receding
questions.explanation: Hot stars radiate more energy at short wavelengths (the blue end), while cooler stars peak at longer wavelengths (the red end), so the colour of a star indicates the area of its spectrum that is most intense — a direct readout of surface temperature. The Sun is a yellow star, neither particularly hot nor cool in the range of star temperatures.

questions.q: A galaxy is at a distance of 6.2 × 10¹⁹ km and is receding at about 1100 km s⁻¹. Calculate Hubble's constant.
working: \(H = \dfrac{v}{d}\)  (Hubble's constant is the gradient of the velocity–distance graph)
The kilometres cancel, leaving inverse seconds:
questions.explanation: Hubble's constant is the recession velocity divided by the distance — the gradient of the velocity-versus-distance graph. Converting the distance into kilometres lets the length units cancel, leaving inverse seconds, which is the giveaway that 1/H will be a time.

questions.q: Using Hubble's constant of 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁷ s⁻¹ and assuming a constant expansion rate, estimate the age of the universe in seconds.
questions.explanation: Assuming a constant expansion rate, the age of the universe is the reciprocal of Hubble's constant. This gives about 1.8 × 10⁹ years — 2 billion years to one significant figure, matching Hubble's original estimate. That figure is famously too young: it is less than the 4.6-billion-year age of the Earth, and Baade's recalibration of Cepheid distances later raised the modern value to about 13.8 billion years.

questions.q: Why is the observation that red-shift is greater for more distant galaxies consistent with an expanding universe?
options: More distant galaxies are intrinsically brighter, so their light is redder
An expanding universe stretches the wavelength of light on its journey, so light from more distant galaxies travels longer and is stretched more, giving greater red-shift
Distant galaxies are made of redder elements than nearby ones
Red-shift is caused by dust between galaxies, which is denser at greater distances
questions.explanation: An expanding universe stretches the wavelength of light on its journey; the longer the light travels, the more it is stretched, so more distant galaxies show greater red-shift. This velocity-proportional-to-distance pattern is the signature of space itself expanding and carrying the galaxies apart, not galaxies merely flying through static space.

questions.q: Using the Doppler effect on a star's absorption lines, what exactly does an astronomer measure, and what does a red-shift indicate?
options: The star's full translational velocity; red-shift means it is approaching
The radial velocity — the component of velocity along the line between observer and star; red-shift means the star is moving away from us
The star's tangential velocity across the sky; red-shift means it is rotating faster
The star's temperature; red-shift means it is hotter
questions.explanation: The Doppler effect shifts a star's absorption lines towards the blue end if it is moving towards us and towards the red end if it is moving away. It measures only the radial velocity — the component of the star's velocity along the line between the observer on Earth and the star. The actual translational velocity is the vector sum of the radial and tangential velocities, so the Doppler shift alone does not give the full speed.

questions.q: Explain why early astronomers wrongly concluded the Sun was mainly composed of iron, and state the correct composition. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The Sun's spectrum contains a very large number of spectral lines, many of them iron lines, which confused astronomers into thinking the Sun was mainly composed of iron. However, the strength of an element's absorption lines depends on the temperature of the star — temperature sets which ionisation states and energy levels are populated, and therefore which lines appear strongly — not simply on the element's abundance. When the temperature dependence of the line strengths is correctly accounted for, the Sun (and stars generally) are shown to be composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, with only a small proportion of heavier elements.

criteria.descriptor: Identifies that the Sun's spectrum has many lines (including strong iron lines), leading to the early iron conclusion.
States that line strength depends on the star's temperature/ionisation state, not abundance alone.
Concludes the Sun is mostly hydrogen and helium.

questions.explanation: The key is that line strength must be interpreted through temperature: the iron lines were strong because the Sun's temperature excites them efficiently, not because iron is abundant. Correcting for this reveals stars are overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium.

questions.q: From memory: a single stellar spectrum carries three separate readings. Using the hook 'Tall Cats Vanish', state each reading and the spectral feature it comes from.
keyPoints: Temperature — from the shape of the continuous background (the blackbody peak / colour): bluer is hotter, redder is cooler.
Composition — from the identity of the absorption lines: which wavelengths the dark lines fall at, matched to laboratory fingerprints of the elements.
Velocity — from the shift of those same lines: redshift means receding, blueshift means approaching, giving the radial velocity only.
questions.explanation: The number-one trap is conflating the three. Burn in the mapping: continuum shape for Temperature, line identity for Composition, line shift for Velocity. If you kept all three distinct, grade Good or Easy.
